Constantine Director 'Hopeful' For Sequel After DC Studios Shakeup
articles.description: The director of Constantine, Francis Lawrence, opened up about the movie's long-awaited sequel now that DC Studios has had a changing of the guard.
articles.content:
The director of Constantine, Francis Lawrence, opened up about the movie's long-awaited sequel now that DC Studios has had a changing of the guard.

James Gunn and Peter Safran are out at DC Studios in a sudden and unexpected move that has sparked no end of worry and speculation among fans. Gunn, for his part, cited a distaste for the “corporate” side of the job, but confirmed that projects already in motion, like Man of Tomorrow, are still a-go.

Fans aren’t the only ones scratching their heads about what might happen next. Francis Lawrence, the director of oodles of Hollywood blockbusters, is also in this boat — though he’s rather optimistic about the situation, as it means he might finally get the chance to make another Constantine film.

Speaking with Collider ahead of his next movie, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Lawrence clarified that he isn’t happy for anyone to lose their jobs, but admitted that he’s keen on the possibility of getting Constantine 2 off the ground now that things are changing at DC.

"Well, I’ll tell you this,” he began. “Not that I want anybody to lose their jobs, so this is not like a schadenfreude kind of thing, but I will say that we’ve been trying to make Constantine 2 for twenty-something years, and we have an idea, and we have a script, and we’ve been wanting to make it, and the people that were at DC were an impediment to us making it.

“So, we are now more hopeful as of yesterday’s news that maybe now there will be another opportunity. But again, we’ve been trying to make this for twenty-something years, and there’s always been obstacles in the road to making it, and it’s not me, it’s not Keanu, it’s not Akiva. J.J. [Abrams] is on it, as well. We all want to do it. So, it’s really going to be people at Paramount, Warner, whoever’s running DC now, getting everybody on board to say, like, 'Hey, we can do a sequel of our version of Constantine?'"

Lawrence said, without a doubt, that this version of Constantine will be another R-Rated film, no matter what. He explained that the first movie had been made with a PG-13 rating in mind, but despite their best efforts, it was hit with an R label. If given the chance to make a sequel, Lawrence wants to lean all-in and make it a true R-Rated experience.

“So, part of the idea from the very beginning was, because we followed all the rules to make a PG-13 movie and we got hit with an R, they told us, 'You can’t do anything about it. It’s going to be an R no matter what.' We tried to fight them on it, and they said, 'Nope. It’s an R,' but really, it’s an R-rated PG-13 movie, which pisses me off,” he explained.

"And so we all kind of came back and said, 'Okay, when we do this next time, we’re making the hard-R version of Constantine.' So when we do it, it’s going to be the hard-R version of Constantine."

Lawrence doubled down on his desire to make another Constantine at all costs, even saying that he doesn’t mind if it gets put into a shared universe or remade to fit DC’s ever-evolving plans at some point. He claimed that he and Keanu would even compromise on their financial compensation to get the film made, if that's what it takes.

"Personally, I don’t even care if somebody has a plan for some sort of shared universe, and they want to do another version of Constantine. If they just let us do the sequel to our version, they can coexist. So, I have renewed hope as of yesterday that there might be some possibility for forward movement there,” he said.

"We have to be responsible,” he continued, speaking about the financial side of the equation. “We want to make it. This is not the kind of movie that I would charge full freight and Keanu could charge full freight. It’s something we have to do, because we love and want to take a gamble on it, and do it responsibly. And so, we’ve been thinking about that same idea for 20 years, that we’re not going to do it for $100 million. We have to be scrappy about it."

Constantine was released in 2005. Starring Keanu Reeves, the movie is based on the DC/Vertigo comic book Hellblazer and follows supernatural detective John Constantine in his mission to purge the world of nefarious evil entities.

This is the latest news about Constantine after Reeves reportedly pitched a sequel to DC Studios in 2025. And just earlier this month, it was revealed that Evil Dead Wrath writer-director Francis Galluppi was hired by DC Studios to write a John Constantine movie for them, though it’s unclear if he’ll also be directing.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Board reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang as second extra-marital affair emerges
articles.description: Nvidia Board reportedly moves to expel Jensen Huang as stock tumbles on latest scandals and lack of succession plans at Nvidia.
articles.content:
Nvidia's Board of Directors is preparing to oust co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang following revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence and another with an Nvidia executive, reports The Wall Street Journal. Although no final decision has been made yet, the company's directors could meet as early as November 11 to discuss Huang's future. Whoever succeeds Huang will be the company's second CEO in 33 years. Nvidia's stock dropped 8% in after-hours trading following the reports. Nvidia's board of directors launched an independent investigation into the matter on November 8.

The report from the WSJ comes hours after the New York Times revealed that Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. According to five people who worked at Nvidia, the relationship was known internally, while Huang and Powell were reportedly seen together at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC conference in March. The allegations follow an earlier report that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

A similar controversy cost Intel chief executive Brian Krzanich his position in June 2018, when an internal investigation confirmed that he had maintained a consensual relationship with an employee, which violated the company's non-fraternization policy applicable to all managers. It is noteworthy that Nvidia's code of conduct explicitly identifies personal relationships as potential conflicts of interest and instructs employees to consult the company's legal department when such conflicts arise. Whether Huang violated Nvidia's internal policies remains unclear, as the code of conduct does not explicitly prohibit all relationships between managers and subordinates.

Huang's potential departure would mark the first CEO transition in Nvidia's 33-year history, and therefore his succession has become an immediate concern for Nvidia, which does not have anyone of Huang's caliber in the leadership team. Although chief financial officer Colette Kress could potentially serve as interim chief executive if Huang is ousted while the BoD searches for a permanent replacement, it remains to be seen how Wall Street would react to this assignment.

Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, who used to be the company's senior vice president of engineering and operations and remains a member of the company's board and an Nvidia Fellow, could also play a role in the succession process, given his extensive knowledge of Nvidia's technology, corporate culture, and history. However, has not served in an executive role at Nvidia for at least a decade, so the chances that he will succeed Huang are low.

Back on Sunday, directors expressed confidence in Jensen Huang and his leadership team, a choice of words that did not exactly guarantee his continued tenure.

articles.title: The 2026 LEGO Star Wars Advent Calendar Is Discounted at Target After Amazon Sells Out
articles.content:
This year's lineup of LEGO Advent Calendars have started going out of stock ahead of Black Friday. Unsurprisingly, the Star Wars-themed calendar is one of the first to have completely disappeared from major retailers. One of the only places you can still buy the set is at Target, and somehow it's still being offered at a nice discount.

If you've been hoping to pick up the 2026 version of this calendar, this is probably your last chance to do so at a discount. Here's a quick rundown of where you can still find this set in stock online.

LEGO Star Wars Advent Calendar Stock Update

Barnes & Noble - $44.99

Macy's - $44.99

Walmart - $52 (3rd-party seller)

Amazon - Out of Stock

LEGO Store - Out of Stock

Best Buy - Out of Stock

Target isn't the only retailer that still has stock available, but it is by far the best deal you'll find online right now. Both Barnes & Noble and Macy's are great places to check for stock after a LEGO set disappears from all other shelves, but it's pretty rare to find discounts on such sets there. Once Target officially sells out of its own inventory, those are the next best places to shop if you want to avoid paying a mark-up.

This year's LEGO Star Wars Advent Calendar is themed after The Mandalorian and Grogu movie, featuring minifigures of The Mandalorian, Grogu, Moff Gideon, Carson Teva, and a Jawa. Most of these characters are also dressed in festive sweaters. You'll also get to build miniature versions of Mando's N-1 Starfighter, The Razor Crest, a Sandcrawler, and more. The set comes with a total of 293 pieces, which is actually 30 more than what we got with the 2025 edition.

When Do LEGO Black Friday Sales Start?

Although most of the LEGO advent calendars will likely sell out before Black Friday actually arrives, we're still expecting better deals on other sets closer to Thanksgiving. Amazon has officially announced that its Black Friday sale will kick off on November 19, which is when most of the really good LEGO discounts will start to arrive. You can also expect the official LEGO Store Black Friday sale to launch on November 27 alongside the new Godzilla set.

articles.title: Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra Is Reportedly 'Close to Done,' Though at the Cost of Cutting Back on Content and Length
articles.description: Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra, Amy Hennig's Captain America/Black Panther game, is reportedly close to being finished, but it sounds like it may be extremely compromised.
articles.content:
Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra, Amy Hennig's Captain America/Black Panther game, is reportedly close to being finished, but it could be extremely compromised.

According to a new report from Kotaku, Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra is "close to done." The news comes hours after rumors began spread online that the game was canceled, with an official announcement coming soon. According to Kotaku and Bloomberg's Jason Schreier, Skydancer leadership told staff via Slack that this is not the case and that they should continue business as usual.

Kotaku's report went on to describe the game's development as difficult, which should come as no surprise to anyone who's been following its journey. The title was announced in 2024 and has been delayed several times, with little to no news or footage beyond that.

Kotaku claims that Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra initially began as a Netflix game, but was later expanded for consoles and PC. Unfortunately, the title is reportedly "light on gameplay," with most of the action mapped to one button and the experience lacking "significant interactivity."

The project has also allegedly gone well over budget, and as a result, has had to "significantly" scale back from its original vision in terms of content and length. As of right now, we have no idea when Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra will release, but if it really is nearing the finish line, we could see something next year. Unfortunately, it doesn't seem like the game will be a hyper-engaging action/adventure title with riveting action, from the sound of it.

This is purely speculative, but based on the details from Kotaku's report, it wouldn't be surprising if this is more along the lines of a Quantic Dream experience like Heavy Rain or Detroit: Become Human, with some combat sprinkled in. Either way, if fans were hoping for something like Marvel's Spider-Man, but with Captain America and Black Panther, they may end up pretty disappointed.

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra is meant to be director Amy Hennig's first proper game since Uncharted 3 in 2011. Although she has consulted and helped out on some other games like Forspoken over the years, Hennig hasn't led a new game since Uncharted 3. She was reportedly ousted from Naughty Dog in the early 2010s after Uncharted 4 was struggling to meet internal expectations. She then went to EA, where she was meant to lead a new Star Wars game with Visceral Games, but the studio was shut down and the project was scrapped. Now, she's heading up this Marvel game... and we'll just have to wait and see how it turns out.

articles.title: AMC App Experiences Slowdown As Marvel Fans Rush to Buy Doomsday Tickets After VisionQuest Finale
articles.description: So many Marvel fans tried to snag their tickets for Avengers: Doomsday after watching the VisionQuest season finale that they literally crashed the AMC Theaters app.
articles.content:
So many Marvel fans tried to snag their tickets for Avengers: Doomsday after watching the VisionQuest season finale that they literally crashed the AMC Theaters app. At least, that's what users are saying.

The crash reportedly occurred on the night of November 10, 2026 — the same night that the VisionQuest finale aired, which included a post-credits scene that all but confirmed a particular character will show up in Avengers: Doomsday.

Shortly after the episode aired on Disney+, fans and Marvel fanpages shared that the AMC app was showing an error message when they tried to use it, which asked them to “please try again.” They were unable to navigate to other pages within the app; it seems that it was totally unusable during this time.

Of course, viewers instantly pointed to the VisionQuest season finale as the reason for this, indicating that the hype levels were high enough to warrant a mass of fan interest in seeing Doomsday in theaters.

In a statement to IGN, an AMC Theaters spokesperson revealed that there was a 30-minute period where "some transactions were taking longer than normal." The spokesperson said that the AMC app didn't outright crash, as data showed that tickets continued to get sold throughout this period, but indicated that some users may have run into that error message during that time.

Warning: Major spoilers for VisionQuest below!

It’s no surprise that Marvel fans got so excited about Doomsday after this; the finale’s post-credits scene, which was also kept a secret from the media, showed Wanda Maximoff, aka the Scarlet Witch, having an interaction with Doctor Doom.

The specific scene returns to the ending of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, in which the Scarlet Witch sacrifices herself by destroying the Darkhold. While viewers were under the impression that her heroic decision ultimately lead to her death, this isn’t the case; Doctor Doom appears and frees her from the rubble that had collapsed on top of her, saying, "Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your power will be mine." She comes to with a shocked expression before the scene ends.

Given that the Scarlet Witch has been officially confirmed to be alive after four years of ambiguity, fans are understandably beside themselves with excitement. On social media, viewers wasted no time sharing their hype for the scene in response to AMC’s app crash, with one writing, “That’s the Scarlet Witch effect!”

“Wanda impact,” another wrote, while another said the crash happened “All because of Wanda Maximoff!”

“Mother is that powerful,” another superfan said. “We’re ready to support anything she does because she can do no wrong.”

IGN has reached out to AMC for comment and will update this article accordingly once communication is received.

Avengers: Doomsday releases in theaters on December 18, 2026; while you’re waiting, you can watch Avengers: Endgame Encore, which has been re-released with new scenes and will be available to stream on Disney+ this Friday.

articles.description: Three days after launching an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang, the Nvidia board is reportedly preparing to oust the executive.
articles.content:
Three days after launching an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang, the Nvidia board is reportedly preparing to oust the executive.

Nvidia's board will be meeting as soon as today to discuss Huang's future after an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, according to The Wall Street Journal. That affair was first reported by The New York Times, and was followed up by a statement issued by Nvidia on Sunday, saying it'd be investigating Jensen Huang. But according to a new report from The New York Times, he'd also engaged in a second affair with an executive who reported to him.

This meeting follows an investigation that was announced on Sunday. In that announcement, Nvidia said, "The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it."

Huang then issued a letter to employees, obtained by The BBC, where he admitted that he was unfaithful and apologized for hurting his wife and children.

In many ways, Jensen Huang is the face of AI in the US, and so it makes sense that Nvidia's board would want to get this situation under control. The company's chips power nearly every AI model that's currently running, and so a security breach of this scale is a massive liability. Huang is a co-founder of Nvidia, and has been running the company since 1993, so his ouster could have huge ramifications.

IGN has reached out to Nvidia for comment, and will update this story as soon as communications have been received.

articles.title: Henry Cavill Is Open to Returning as Superman Once Again
articles.description: Henry Cavill has stated that he's still open to the idea of playing Superman following all the shake-ups at DC Studios.
articles.content:
Henry Cavill has stated that he's still open to the idea of playing Superman following all the shake-ups at DC Studios.

In an interview with Inverse, Cavill was asked if he'd ever be interested in playing Superman again, and the interviewer suggested the Kingdom Come storyline as a possibility. Cavill noted he would never say never to the idea, and that there are a lot of "fantastic storylines" to adapt for Superman.

"Look, there's lots of fantastic storylines. There's always a lot of opportunity. As the pigeon sang to Fievel in An American Tail, 'never say never.' And I buy into that. I’ve had such a wonderful time playing Superman in the past. I would never say never now."

Of course, the timing of these comments could not come at a more interesting moment. If this happened a week ago, no one would've thought much of it. However, earlier this week, DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran were ousted from the company. They remain on board until December 1, when a new head, Jeremy Latcham, will take over. Latcham is expected to make changes to DC's direction, possibly resulting in a reboot, though that has yet to be firmly decided. His ultimate vision, however, is to focus on DC's mainstream characters in an effort to quickly assemble the Justice League on the big screen.

Presumably, they'll wait until James Gunn's Superman sequel, Man of Tomorrow, hits theaters in July to make a decision on whether they'll reboot or recast this DC universe. Cavill has famously been through a lot as Superman. His debut film, Man of Steel, was controversial thanks to the absurd casualties in his fight with General Zod. Batman v Superman also caused some friction with fans for a variety of reasons, one of which was that Superman was extremely brooding and miserable.

After the catastrophic disaster that was Justice League, Cavill's role as Superman remained in question. There were rumors he would be replaced, while others indicated the powers that be simply weren't sure what to do with him. Eventually, Dwayne 'The Rock' Johnson went above all of the WB execs and brought the actor back for a cameo in 2022's Black Adam, five years after Cavill's last appearance in the role. He was promised new Superman adventures... but then, James Gunn took over DC just weeks later, and Cavill was essentially let go from the role.

The fact that Cavill is open to taking another crack at things after all of that is certainly interesting. Whether that opportunity ever comes remains to be seen, but it seems hard to imagine the new leadership reviving the Snyderverse.

articles.title: A Death Metal Guitarist Is So Into WoW Forever, He Took it Onstage With a Steam Deck
articles.description: World of Warcraft Forever is off to a monumental start, with more players wandering Azeroth than ever before. And at least one death metal guitarist can't put it down long enough to watch his opener play.
articles.content:
World of Warcraft Forever is off to a monumental start, with more players wandering Azeroth than ever before. And at least one death metal guitarist can't put it down long enough to watch his opener play.

Death metal band Archspire posted a video to Instagram, overlaid with text that reads, "POV World of Warcraft Forever comes out the same day as the show," as the camera shows a Steam Deck with an undead Warlock running around with his voidwalker. The caption carries on the bit, saying, "When your set starts at 9:00 but you just zoned into Undercity to pick up your Voidwalker quest so you can pet-tank your way through Fenris Isle."

I get the appeal, some of the quests in Fenris Isle are absolutely brutal if you don't have anyone else in your party, so getting a purple blob that can tank it for you really is exciting. It doesn't hurt that WoW Forever runs incredibly on a handheld, either.

WoW Forever's newfound controller support and lightweight system requirements make it a natural match for handheld gaming PCs. I've tested the game on both the Xbox Ally X and the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, and both have been able to handle the game at pretty high settings without dipping below 60 fps. I haven't played the game on the Steam Deck quite yet, but at least from Archspire's Instagram post, it seems to be running just fine.

Archspire's guitarist is also not the only Death Metaller who loves WoW. IGN interviewed Cannibal Corpse way back in 2008, and when we asked George "Corpsegrinder" Fisher about his love for the game, he told us, "It is true, I am obsessed with WOW! I have 70 level 70 characters. I play HORDE side ONLY. I hate the Alliance with a passion!"

Corpsegrinder also told us a story about how he was inundated with messages from fans, saying, "I did another interview where I said my Rogue's name and the server I played on, and then I started getting tells in game. A LOT OF TELLS. I was getting bombarded even when I was raiding, so I transferred him off the server and changed his name. I loved talking to people who were into Cannibal Corpse, but it was getting so I logged in and couldn't play, because all I did was exchange tells with people."

A lot has changed since 2008, but WoW Forever is looking to recapture some of that old-school WoW magic. And just based on how many people are playing the game, Blizzard seems to have pulled it off, even though they've run into some hurdles with gold rewards and dungeon experience.

articles.title: New Mega Man Legends Game, Movie, or TV Series Possibly In the Works After Fans Spot 'New Media' Listing
articles.description: A now-deleted listing for ‘Mega Man Legends — New Media’ was spotted on a ‘What’s Shooting’ page for ACTRA Toronto, hinting that a new game, film, or TV series in the franchise's 'Legends' series is in the works.
articles.content:
A now-deleted listing for ‘Mega Man Legends — New Media’ was spotted on a ‘What’s Shooting’ page for ACTRA Toronto, hinting that a new game, film, or TV series in the franchise's 'Legends' series is in the works.

Although it’s since been deleted, several publications were able to screenshot the listing before it was taken down. The project’s start date was listed as September 14, 2026, with an end date of December 1, 2026. Casting was listed as “in-house.”

ACTRA Toronto’s What’s Shooting page is a public database that compiles ongoing projects that are registered with Canada’s performers’ union, the Alliance of Canadian Cinema, Television and Radio Artists. The Mega Man project’s ‘New Media’ label is especially intriguing, as this doesn’t necessarily denote that a new game is being made; rather, it’s vague enough to encompass any manner of projects, including movies or TV shows.

A Mega Man Legends movie isn’t out of the question, especially given Capcom’s recent foray into the world of Hollywood films. Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil adaptation was wildly successful, and hopes are high for a sequel to Legendary’s Street Fighter flick. In fact, Capcom has been working toward a screen adaptation of Mega Man for some time; the developer confirmed that a movie was being made in 2018, which was initially being handled by 20th Century Fox (now 20th Century Studios).

Things were quiet for the next few years until 2020, when Henry Joost and Ariel Schulman, who were set to write and direct this movie, confirmed that it was still very much in production.

“We are super excited about it. I think we’re going to have some big news about it soon. I can’t say all that much right now, but it’s a project very near and dear to our hearts and we’re psyched,” Joost said at the time.

In 2021, Netflix announced that it was making a live action film based on Capcom’s legacy 2D platformer, which appeared to be unrelated to 20th Century’s Mega Man project. For now, it’s unclear if this newest listing is involved with either of those productions, and the slim information that's been provided is making fans' imaginations run wild.

Of course, most players are keen for a Mega Man Legends remake, or at least another title in that particular series. The first Mega Man Legends game was released all the way back in 1998; a sequel came out in 2000, and a spin-off title, The Misadventures of Tron Bonne, launched in 1999. With Dual Override coming in 2027, and Capcom expressing an interest in reviving its older IP, it’s certainly possible that there’s already another Mega Man title in the works — and remakes of legacy games are proving to be a real hit right now, after all.

For now, Mega Man fans can check out our interview with Dual Override’s Director Shinya Ikuta, Producer Hiroyuki Minamitani, Art Director Yuji Ishihara, and Art Director Shinsuke Komaki, where we asked them all about the game and what players can expect when it finally releases.

articles.title: Jamie Campbell Bower Calls Rings of Power Season 3 the 'Perfect Kind of Antidote' After Stranger Things
articles.description: The character of Celeborn -- Jamie Campbell Bower's first role after playing Vecna, et al, in Seasons 4 and 5 of Stranger Things -- helped the actor move on from those persistently dark characters.
articles.content:
Jamie Campbell Bower has not been coy about Stranger Things being an emotionally taxing gig. As Vecna (and all of his many iterations) in the final two seasons of the Netflix series, Bower would put himself through intense and isolating experiences in preparation of playing the show's big bad. At MegaCon in early 2025, months ahead of the Stranger Things series finale, Bower said that he told his therapist that he wouldn't "be doing another bad guy for a minute" because it "f---s me up."

Bower's first post-Stranger Things role is, appropriately, miles away from his characters' persistent darkness. He's now starring in the third season of Prime Video's Rings of Power, which picks up five years after Season 2 well into the battle with Sauron, as Galadriel's long-lost husband, the elf Celeborn. Morfydd Clark's Galadriel mentions in Season 1 that Celeborn had not returned from his battle with Morgoth. In Season 3, the semi-estranged couple is reunited. On the red carpet for the season premiere in New York, Bower said that playing Celeborn was refreshing.

"I've been describing it as the perfect kind of antidote, I suppose," he told IGN. "It is so different to what I was doing before, and I'm so grateful to be here and so grateful to join this amazing cast and crew and this world. It's been beautiful. It really has been. It's been gorgeous."

Bower also elaborated on playing a character who has more ambiguity. J.R.R. Tolkien wrote several versions of Celeborn's origins, but never settled on one definitively. Thanks to the murkiness of of Tolkien's legendarium, the many depictions of Celeborn in adapted media and Tolkien's own writings left room for the actor to interpret the elf in his own way.

"Celeborn's really interesting because he was approached and then kind of re-approached in the works. And so there has been sort of... not conflicting, but different information that's available on him," he said. "My job was realistically to take what was there, look at what I related to, look at what was obvious, and then build on top of that. And I think for me as an actor, my intention was really to come into it with sensitivity and a vulnerability for him, which has been beautiful. It's been great."

We haven't seen too much of Celeborn in Season 3 yet, only appearing in a flashback meeting Galadriel 1,000 years ago in Episode 1 and again in Episode 4 (no spoilers), but it sure seems freeing to be able to act without prosthetics from day one.

We're liking Season 3 so far, giving the first batch of episodes an 8 in our review and calling it "a new beginning for the Prime Video series [...], streamlining the overall narrative into a more cohesive war story" that "refocuses The Rings of Power on its simple yet compelling good vs. evil premise, jettisoning some past characters and subplots while ensuring the ones remaining all align with the same goal: you exist to either defeat Sauron or to serve him."

Rings of Power Season 3 Episodes 1–4 is available to stream on Prime Video now. Episodes 5 and 6 premiere November 18, and Episodes 7 and 8 come out November 25.

articles.title: Jensen Huang now accused of affair with Nvidia executive who reported to him, alleged cover-up attempt
articles.description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly had an extramarital affair with a direct report, following a separate affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
articles.content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — already embroiled in a scandal for an extramarital relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence to be spying on behalf of China — reportedly had a separate affair with one of his direct reports, according to the New York Times. Nvidia's board is now reportedly preparing to fire Huang.

The Times, citing five anonymous sources within Nvidia, says that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of health care. The sources claim that Huang and Powell were "captured on video being affectionate" in March at a hotel in San Jose, Calif., where the company's GTC conference takes place.

That report says that someone at the hotel filmed the moment on their smartphone, but that Huang's security team "sequestered" them and "made the person an offer to sign a nondisclosure agreement."

Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and has been steadily promoted. The Times highlights that personal relationships are mentioned as potentially causing conflicts of interest in Nvidia's code of conduct. Like Huang, she is married to someone else.

In 2018, former Intel CEO Brian Krzanich resigned following a relationship with an employee, which was also against the company's policies. Nvidia has not responded to a request for comment from Tom's Hardware. This story will be updated if we hear back.

Earlier this week, it came out that Jensen had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, formerly a top executive at Singaporean firm Megaspeed and believed by U.S. intelligence to be a spy. Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia employees. China has denied claims of espionage.

Nvidia's board has an ongoing investigation into that affair, led by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. Huang is continuing to run the company while that investigation is ongoing. Law firms have been racing to sue the company on behalf of shareholders, including a proposed class-action lawsuit that Nvidia misled investors on material facts about the business.

The Congressional House committee on China has called on Huang for a closed-door session, with Republican lawmakers saying the reports "raise significant national security concerns."

Huang has been a leader of the AI industry, providing the most sought-after chips in the field. He has also had the ear of President Donald Trump, traveling with him and attempting to influence export controls.

Trump told reporters that the FBI was investigating Huang, but also that the Nvidia CEO "had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

articles.title: Final Fantasy XIV Players Mourn The Primals Bassist With In-Game Funerals and Gatherings
articles.description: Final Fantasy XIV players are paying tribute to the bassist of the game’s official band, mourning him and celebrating his legacy with virtual, in-game funerals across servers worldwide.
articles.content:
Final Fantasy XIV players are paying tribute to the bassist of the game’s official band, mourning him and celebrating his legacy with virtual, in-game funerals across servers worldwide.

Eikichi Iwai was the bass guitarist for The Primals, a band formed specifically to make some of the music in Square Enix’s extremely popular MMORPG. While they aren’t the only ones responsible for some of the game’s iconic tunes, they’re certainly some of the most notable, and they’ve become a firm fixture in the Final Fantasy fanbase over the years.

Iwai’s death was officially announced on November 11, 2026 by his own rock band, Chirinuruwowa, and the Final Fantasy XIV development team, the latter of which penned a public letter to fans informing them of the news.

“As announced earlier today, we are deeply saddened to share the news of the sudden passing of bassist Eikichi Iwai,” the statement reads. “Having witnessed his truly unforgettable performance on stage at the recent FINAL FANTASY XIV Fan Festival in Japan, the sudden news of his passing has come as a profound shock. The members of THE PRIMALS and the entire FFXIV Development and Operations teams are overcome with deep sorrow.

“As we reflect on all that Eikichi-san has left behind, our thoughts are with him, and we offer our heartfelt condolences.”

Chirinuruwowa published a similar statement on social media. “We regret to inform you that our bassist, Iwaieikichi, has passed away suddenly,” the group wrote. “The sudden news of his passing has left all of us in the band and on the staff struggling to come to terms with it, and we are deeply saddened.” The band also informed fans that all upcoming performances in their Endless Loop 2026 -Public- tour have been cancelled.

Iwai's death sent shockwaves throughout the FFXIV playerbase. In acknowledgement of his legacy as a performer and paying tribute to his contributions to the game, these players gathered together within their respective servers to hold virtual funerals in some of the MMORPG’s fantastical locales.

For example, players on the European server Omega formed a circle around Limsa Lominsa’s Aetheryte Plaza, lighting campfires in remembrance of the bassist. And in the Sephirot, Materia DC server, players hung out for more than seven hours at Ultima Thule, calmly sitting in its field of flowers.

Fans, content creators, and fellow members of the games industry have shared their own fond memories of the game and the impact Iwai's music had on their lives.

articles.title: CD Projekt Red Used AI to Alter Geralt's Voice Due to Polish Actor's Health Issues
articles.description: The Witcher 3 is getting a new expansion more than 11 years after it first released, and due to a health issue experienced by Geralt's Polish voice actor, CD Projekt Red will be using an AI tool to modify his voice.
articles.content:
The Witcher 3 is getting a new expansion more than 11 years after it first released, and due to a health issue experienced by Geralt's Polish voice actor, CD Projekt Red will be using an AI tool to modify his voice.

Jacek Rozenek, who voiced Geralt in The Witcher 3's Polish dub, will be returning to voice Geralt in Songs of the Past. Rozenek notably suffered a stroke back in 2019 that affected his voice. Thanks to modern technology, CD Projekt Red is able to use an AI voice modulator, Respeecher, to alter the actor's voice to match his 2014 lines, as noted by Game File.

According to the post, Rozenek's stroke left him unable to even speak for a while, and he only gained his voice back after a ton of rigorous training. He was able to return for a couple of quests in the Next-Gen update that came out back in 2022, but told Game File that he "was so exhausted after this recording." Still, CD Projekt Red wanted him to return for the new expansion, so it had to think outside the box.

The main problem was that, after everything Rozenek went through, his voice was noticably different than it was in 2014 when he recorded the bulk of Geralt's lines for the original game. Rozenek's voice is now much lower pitched than it used to be, which would make any new lines sound odd when played next to the older ones that are supposed to take place in the same time period. Hence, the need for Respeecher.

Respeecher's model was trained on all of Rozenek's lines from the original game, but it sounds like this was doing a lot more than just running his voice through a quick filter. When asked about the process, Respeecher synthetic speech artist Dmytro Vasylets told Game File that "getting there took dozens of hours, training models, going through the details with the CDPR team, and dealing with AI artifacts that never fully disappear."

CDPR got Rozenek's blessing to use the tool, who told Game File, "I have great trust… for the creators of this game," and that, "when it comes to the dynamics of the voice, when it comes to the acting aspects, I feel very good, really very good."

Still, CDPR is aware of the optics of using AI anywhere near a voice actor, and it stressed to Game File that this was a special case. CD Projekt Red localization producer Mikołaj Szwed told the publication that the company wouldn't be using any AI tools to alter someone's voice without the express permission of that voice actor.

Even for The Witcher 4, which Rozenek is expected to return for, the tool won't be needed, due to Geralt being older and more grizzled, so a deeper voice won't be so jarring.

But while this seems like a good use of AI, the technology is still extremely controversial in gaming. Last year, the Indie Game Awards stripped the Game of the Year award from Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 after AI-generated placeholder textures were found in the game. Players have also found AI-generated art in Crimson Desert, though it's since been patched out.

articles.title: AMD’s Venice-X maxes out family at 5.3 GHz, returning 3D V-Cache to data center after four years
articles.description: AMD's Venice-X CPUs launch in the second half of 2027, bringing 3D V-Cache back to the data center after four years on the sidelines.
articles.content:
AMD missed out on deploying Turin-X CPUs in the previous generation, giving its 3D V-Cache tech a four-year hiatus from the data center following the launch of Genoa-X in 2023. In the second half of next year, 3D V-Cache is coming back for HPC with Venice-X, matching the 96 cores and 1,152 MB of L3 cache available on the EPYC 9684X (Genoa-X), but with vastly higher clock speeds, PCIe 6.0, and nearly four times the per-socket memory bandwidth.

After first bringing hybrid bonding to EPYC processors with Milan-X in 2022, AMD followed up a little over a year later with Genoa-X. Turin came and went without a chip sporting stacked SRAM, but now, it’s back with Venice-X. The critical change this time around doesn’t come from big jumps in core count — and consequently cache — as is the case with the standard SP7 lineup. Rather, it’s the 5.3 GHz boost clock speed, another pillar of Venice broadly, that’s particularly beneficial in the HPC workloads Venice-X targets.

As you can see from the top EPYC -X chips from previous generations, boost clocks were significantly lower for the X chips, and higher frequencies were available within the standard chips from each family. Milan scaled up to 4.1 GHz, while Genoa could climb to 4.4 GHz, just not on the EPYC -X chips. Venice-X brings up to the maximum 5.3 GHz boost clock available across the range, unifying a high frequency with a large pool of bonded L3 for HPC workloads.

There are still details missing about Venice-X, including the base frequency, how many SKUs are in the lineup and what their specs are, and the TDP (though the 400 to 600 W range available to other Venice CPUs is likely). The chips appear to use the SP7 socket, however, keeping with previous EPYC -X chips.

The platform comes with 96 PCIe 6.0 lanes, while the smaller SP8 platform targeting enterprises trades memory channels for PCIe lanes. Venice-X comes with the full 16-channel memory setup available on SP7, including support for MRDIMMs at 12,800 MT/s that can drive the quoted 1.6 TB/s of per-socket memory bandwidth.

The critical marriage with Venice-X for HPC workloads, according to AMD, is high frequency with a large pool of stacked cache. AMD currently maintains both 3D V-Cache and high-frequency EPYC chips in its HPC fleet to run its internal EDA workloads. AMD Fellow Phil Steinke says the company runs performance analysis on these workloads to characterize performance, optimize EPYC designs, and push partners to optimize their software.

The biggest consumer on the HPC fleet by far are function verification workloads at over half of AMD's used compute, according to Steinke. These are logic simulations that show up in tools like Cadence Xcelium, and Steinke says the EPYC team is running these workloads “24 x 7 x 365.”

(Image credit: AMD) An example of one such workload is above, measuring IPC with AMD's uProf monitoring utility. With 3D V-Cache, AMD says this workload completes 40% faster at around double the instructions per clock. AMD didn't clarify which chips it was comparing or what application it was using. However, the comparison is between an EPYC fleet with and without 3D V-Cache.

Steinke says AMD is able to now move toward a single chip with Venice-X, maintaining the cache advantages in workloads like functional verification while driving the EDA workloads more sensitive to frequency. "I mentioned we have a mix of high frequency and 3D V-Cache CPUs in our data center, and that's because through Milan and Genoa, the high frequency parts were always a little higher on the frequency side," Steinke said. "You don't have that dichotomy [with Venice-X]. You can get the best of both worlds in a single CPU, and this is what we're really excited to be picking up for our own use."

AMD hasn't shared any benchmarks for Venice-X yet, but it provided some more specific HPC benchmarks comparing its high-frequency EPYC 9686F to Intel's Xeon 6980P in several HPC workloads, such as computational fluid dynamics. In AMD's testing, the 9686F was 1.6x faster in these benchmarks while running 32 fewer cores.

(Image credit: AMD) We had a chance to test the EPYC 9686F along with the dense EPYC 9996, which you can read more about in our Zen 6 EPYC Venice deep dive and benchmarking article. And indeed, the EPYC 9686F looks very impressive in some of the HPC workloads we ran.

(Image credit: Tom's Hardware) We were only able to test a 2P configuration, and as evidenced by the sole Xeon 6980P, CloverLeaf is sensitive to latency. Even then, the 2P EPYC 9686F completed the complex hydrodynamics simulation in about a third of the time as a single Xeon 6980P.

AMD says it's currently using MEXT, its AI-driven flash-as-DRAM technology, to bolster the amount of memory available for its EDA workloads. When it deploys Venice-X, Steinke says the company will continue using MEXT, which you can read more about in our recent MEXT breakdown on Tom's Hardware Premium.

Venice-X CPUs are launching in the second half of 2027, while SP7 and SP8 Venice CPUs are rolling out now. Also coming in the second half of next year is AMD's Verano, which it's pitching as an AI host node that leverages SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X memory.

articles.title: Prusa launches new carbon-fiber and carbon-nanotube-filled 3D printing filament for electronics manufacturing
articles.description: Prusament PETG ESD is the cheapest ESD filament on the market, while being carbon-fiber reinforced, something the competition doesn't have.
articles.content:
Prusa released its new Prusament PETG ESD on Tuesday: a carbon-fiber and carbon-nanotube (CNT)- filled, electrostatic-dissipative (ESD) PETG filament meant to protect static-sensitive electronics. While it’s great for enclosures for a Raspberry Pi, ESP32, and the like, Prusa is targeting the filament more toward electronics production than hobbyist use; however, it’s cheaper than the non-ESD Prusament PETG Carbon Fiber at only $56.99.

Prusament PETG ESD Black 1kg - $56.99

Prusa isn’t the only one selling ESD filament; 3DXTech and Polymaker were first to the scene, but Prusa is the first to include carbon fiber alongside carbon nanotubes to provide the ESD properties, improving dimensional accuracy and minimizing warping. 3DXTech sells its ESD-PETG at $105; Polymaker’s Fiberon PETG-ESD is $65.98, but the Prusament PETG ESD is only $56.99 and is the only one with carbon fiber reinforcement.

Non-ESD filaments are generally safe for electronics enclosures; many hobbyists use regular PLA, PETG, and ABS without any problems. And while the extra protection can be appreciated, Prusa positions this not for hobbyists, but for electronics production — PCB fixtures and holders for soldering, IC trays for handling and transport, holders for testing multiple boards at once, etc., as Prusa shows on the PETG ESD product page. It saves on manufacturing costs, reducing the need for CNC-machined ESD trays and fixtures, and can be quickly printed on-site with very little lead time. It’s not necessarily for big businesses only either, as indie hardware developers and smaller-scale manufacturers could use this filament to improve their production line without buying expensive ESD filament.

Prusa has not yet published the datasheet containing details about the strength of the filament, but Prusa claims that the filament has increased stiffness and reduced toughness, similar to Prusament PETG Carbon Fiber’s properties. However, the amount of carbon fiber in PETG ESD may be different from PETG Carbon Fiber, as the latter’s purpose is more for strength than for electronics manufacturing.

Prusa is known to use its own 3D printers to print its own components and use its own products for the 3D printers it sells, and on the product page, Prusa says it uses PETG ESD in its own production line to prevent overcoating the edges when powder coating its print sheets. While it isn’t the first or only ESD filament on the market, it’s certainly the cheapest, and when its strength profile is released or tested independently, it may potentially be more worth it than Prusa’s own PETG Carbon Fiber in certain cases.

articles.title: New GTA 6 Surprise Gameplay Seemingly Released in Yet Another Viral Marketing Stunt
articles.description: Rockstar Games appears to have released new footage from GTA 6, which also recreates the studio's real-life viral marketing in-game.
articles.content:
Rockstar Games appears to have released new footage from GTA 6, which also recreates the studio's real-life viral marketing in-game.

A new Instagram post from the account "Only in Dade" began to raise eyebrows earlier today, as it appeared to contain legitimate footage of GTA 6. The footage shows someone driving down Ocean Drive, recording a bunch of flashy cars lined up while people wander past. A second person on the sidewalk recorded the exact same video from a different perspective. Some fans think that the two people recording are Jason and Lucia, respectively, though the footage isn't clear enough to be able to confidently make that determination.

Many were wondering if this was AI footage or a render until Rockstar Games reposted it on its Instagram story and liked the video, indicating this is likely real in-game footage. The studio is very careful and calculated with what it chooses to post and interact with, so it isn't going around liking random AI-generated clips of its upcoming game.

However, what's even more interesting is that this footage directly recreates a real-life video from last month. Rockstar teamed up with West Coast Customs to bring cars from GTA 6 to real life and spent October parading them around the city of Miami. As a result, there were tons of videos and social media posts about these vehicles, and one has now seemingly been recreated in GTA 6. You can see the same people, including a person on a motorized scooter and a man taking pictures in front of one of the cars, all replicated in the GTA 6 footage above.

It's clear that Rockstar's marketing strategy has gotten extremely creative, and it's a bit of a flex to produce something that has many wondering if the visuals are too good to be true. Rockstar also pulled off a similar stunt a couple of weeks ago when it debuted a tiny bit of new gameplay during an episode of South Park. The footage wasn't advertised ahead of time, so people also thought that it might be AI-generated gameplay until Rockstar's name was discovered in the credits.

The hype for GTA 6 is currently at its peak, releasing in just one week. The launch represents the end of a 13-year journey for many fans, as Rockstar hasn't made a new GTA game since 2013. There was, of course, Red Dead Redemption 2 in 2018, which certainly helped tide some fans over... but that was still nearly a decade ago at this point.

Pre-loading has officially begun so fans can prepare for their trip to Vice City next week. Rockstar has also released new trailers, screenshots, and other marketing beats, which have created a flury of speculation over what may or may not be in the game. Thankfully, we won't have to wait much longer to find out.

articles.title: Anthropic built a model that beats Opus. It recommends Opus anyway.
articles.description: Anthropic just released a coding model that beats Opus 5.5 on two major benchmarks and can complete certain difficult tasks The post Anthropic built a model that beats Opus. It recommends Opus anyway. appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
Anthropic just released a coding model that beats Opus 5.5 on two major benchmarks and can complete certain difficult tasks for half the cost.

Yet in its Fable 5.2 announcement on Monday, the company recommended that most developers stick with Opus, calling it the “strongest daily driver” for coding and knowledge work.

“Based on capabilities and pricing, Claude Opus 5.5 is still our recommended model for most everyday work, from coding to knowledge work,” Anthropic tells The New Stack.

“Based on capabilities and pricing, Claude Opus 5.5 is still our recommended model for most everyday work, from coding to knowledge work.”

Anthropic says Fable is intended for large software migrations, multi-agent builds and long-running research, but its performance data complicates the recommendation. The more expensive model can cost less to complete certain tasks, and the company’s proposed multi-model architecture adds considerations around delegation, context management, and execution costs.

When pricier runs cheaper

On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored 45.3%, nearly matching Opus 5.5’s best result of 45.5%, while completing the benchmark tasks at roughly half the cost, according to Anthropic.

Fable costs twice as much per token, at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens compared with Opus at $4 and $20, yet its reported task cost was lower, demonstrating that token pricing alone doesn’t determine which model is more economical.

Anthropic also cited an internal experiment in which 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours. With the same agent configuration, Opus 5.5 completed only 26% after 18 hours and made little additional progress by the 30-hour mark, according to the company’s published results.

The experiment demonstrates the scale of work Anthropic is targeting with Fable, although it doesn’t establish how much of that advantage carries over to smaller deployments or conventional coding workloads.

Model manager mode

The company is also positioning Fable as a coordinator for less expensive models, so developers can reserve reasoning capabilities for work that other models cannot reliably complete.

“Fable 5.2 can act as an orchestrator that delegates simpler tasks to Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5, or as an advisor those models consult on harder problems.”

“Developers also no longer have to choose just one model,” Anthropic tells The New Stack, “Fable 5.2 can act as an orchestrator that delegates simpler tasks to Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5, or as an advisor those models consult on harder problems.”

For a large software migration, Fable could analyze dependencies, plan changes across services, and delegate individual implementation tasks to Opus or Sonnet. More difficult decisions could then be escalated back to Fable without requiring the more expensive model to perform every step.

Coinbase has already built a multi-model infrastructure that routes tasks based on requirements and cost, and the company says it cut internal AI spending by nearly half even as token usage increased.

Anthropic wants Fable to handle some of those routing decisions itself, although any savings will depend on how often cheaper models can finish the work they’re assigned without needing help, since additional model calls, context transfers and failed attempts can drive up costs over the course of a long-running agent task.

The context-switching tax

There’s another complication when developers switch between models during a conversation. Fable 5.2 can read thinking blocks generated by Opus 5.5, but Opus cannot read those generated by Fable.

This could mean finding another way to pass along relevant context when building systems that move work between models, something that can require additional tokens, not to mention eat into the savings from using cheaper models.

Switch sooner, save more

Anthropic recommends starting with Opus and moving to Fable when higher-effort Opus evaluations fail to meet a project’s requirements, providing a capability-based switching rule that doesn’t necessarily account for the lowest total execution cost.

Its FrontierCode results show Fable achieving comparable performance at roughly half the task cost, so it is probable developers could benefit from switching earlier than Anthropic recommends.

Nvidia this week donated OpenShell, its open-source runtime for securing and governing AI agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. The teams that run it in production already work with Kubernetes and the CNCF’s other projects, says Ali Golshan, Nvidia’s senior director of AI software, who leads the project.

The company announced the move on Tuesday at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City. OpenShell, which Nvidia launched at its GTC conference in March, joins the CNCF as a Sandbox project, the foundation’s entry-level tier for early-stage projects. The CNCF formally accepted the project in late September.

The CNCF currently hosts 262 projects, including 155 at the Sandbox level, but it wasn’t the only possible home for OpenShell. The CNCF’s parent organization, the Linux Foundation, also runs the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), which hosts agentgateway, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol. Last month, the AAIF also took in OpenSandbox, a sandbox platform for AI agents that Alibaba contributed.

“Securing and creating trust around AI is really infrastructure. That’s really where you need to start.”

But as Golshan tells The New Stack, “Securing and creating trust around AI is really infrastructure. That’s really where you need to start.” That, he says, is what made the CNCF the logical place for the project to land.

The platform team is the user

OpenShell runs an agent inside a sandbox and enforces policies on which files, networks, credentials, and model endpoints that agent can reach. That enforcement happens in the infrastructure around the agent, according to the CNCF, and the project is adopting Cedar, another CNCF project, as its policy language.

Golshan says that securing agents takes a full stack solution and that Nvidia couldn’t build that stack one piece at a time.

“We can’t go build OpenShell and then go build the next pieces of it,” he says. “And a lot of those pieces, from an infrastructure standpoint, already existed in CNCF.” He cites Kubernetes itself, as well as the lightweight K3s distribution and service meshes, as examples of adjacent projects.

While building OpenShell, it also became clearer who would operate it, Golshan says. The profile matched the DevSecOps engineer who already stands up the rest of a company’s infrastructure.

He points to SAP as a company where DevOps and infrastructure teams stand up large agent environments.

The people who work with the agents may be engineers or researchers, he says, but the operators are “the same teams that are spinning up Kube and Linux and that whole stack.”

Ideally, those end users never see OpenShell. “You don’t really see Kubernetes,” Golshan says. “You just get that environment.”

When Jonathan Bryce, the CNCF’s executive director, thinks about where a technology should live, he tells The New Stack, the question to ask is “where are the people who are going to be making the decision about deploying, using, contributing to a specific technology?”

Agents started with people running OpenClaw on Mac Minis at home, Bryce says, but long-running, SaaS-style agents look more like other software run in a data center. Before OpenShell joined the CNCF, he adds, much of its early uptake came from neoclouds, GPU cloud providers that want to govern the workloads their customers run on their infrastructure.

Since OpenShell plugs into Kubernetes and other ecosystem projects, Bryce says, teams that already run that stack can easily add it to the workloads they want to contain.

Where agent projects live

Agents will exist throughout the entire stack, Bryce says, and the open-source projects that support them will spread across several foundations, each with a different kind of contributor.

The PyTorch Foundation, home to PyTorch, vLLM, DeepSpeed, and Ray, is where the engineers with deep AI expertise work. Bryce likens them to “the people who write Postgres.”

The CNCF, he says, is “the very broad set of folks who understand how to take mature systems and deploy, scale, observe, secure them.”

The AAIF, with protocols like MCP and A2A, is oriented toward the front-end experience of agents, Bryce says. He compares those protocols to HTTP and JavaScript, the standards that made millions of web apps possible.

The foundations are “Venn diagrams” and not silos, Bryce says, “and I think that’s good.” He points to KubeRay, which runs Ray workloads on Kubernetes, and to llm-d, which pairs vLLM with Kubernetes. The AAIF’s agentgateway works with Kubernetes, too.

The CNCF also tends to be flexible about where a project lands and lets maintainers “choose their own adventure to some extent,” he notes.

Meanwhile, Bryce says Nvidia’s visibility into how people run AI workloads is “unparalleled,” and the company brings new projects built on that experience to each KubeCon. “Some of those end up in a foundation,” he says. “Some of them don’t.”

Governance and a security committee

Golshan joined Nvidia in 2025, when the company acquired Gretel, the synthetic data startup he co-founded. Before that, he also co-founded StackRox, the Kubernetes security company Red Hat acquired in 2021.

He says the people who started OpenShell had been contributors to CNCF projects and knew its governance model from the inside.

That model fit what the team wanted, he says: a single mission for OpenShell and a place within a larger ecosystem.

Security governance, he says, is still being worked out. OpenShell is a Sandbox project for now, and Golshan says the team is “spending a bunch of time thinking through” how to put an independent security committee around it.

“One of the things that I think becomes very important is how do you manage things like disclosures, vulnerabilities,” he says. If OpenShell is going to become a critical piece of infrastructure, he adds, it needs contributions from many participants, “not necessarily us.”

Nvidia’s engineers will keep working on the project’s core, but Red Hat, Docker, and Canonical have been core contributors alongside Nvidia since the start.

When Nvidia opened OpenShell for early access in March, roughly 10 to 15 companies were contributing, Golshan says. The project dropped its alpha label with the 0.1.0 release in September, and the CNCF’s project page now lists about 380 contributing organizations.

“There are a lot of people who will engage at a certain level without it being in neutral governance,” Bryce says. “But once it makes that move to fully neutral governance, then that engagement gets a lot deeper.”

Adoption cycles that used to take two or three years now play out in six to 12 months, Bryce says, and he describes neutral governance as “rocket fuel” for integration and adoption.

“llm-d came into CNCF in March of this year, and they now have their 1.0 release,” Bryce says of the distributed inference framework, “and they have a whole set of companies that are actually running it in production, including some of the neoclouds.”

What Nvidia wants from the community

Golshan says OpenShell needs an ecosystem of tools around it before it can run at scale in production. About 50 to 60 companies, from startups to large vendors, have built on it so far, he says. OpenShell now has defined extension points for compute, credential management, inference providers, and policy enforcement, and he hopes the CNCF community will use them as a blueprint for tying OpenShell into the rest of the cloud native stack.

“It would be amazing if within the next six months we could support everything from Istio to Envoy to K3s for edge,” Golshan says.

Since the 0.1.0 release, early adopters that are moving agents from research into production have asked for recommendations on security, privacy, and observability tooling that works natively with OpenShell, he says. They also want help optimizing the agents and harnesses that run inside it.

Golshan describes a recent conversation in Berlin with someone who already knew Datadog and distributed tracing well. “I don’t even know what to observe for an agent,” he recalls the person saying.

Golshan wants what the community learns from those edge cases to flow back into the OpenShell core, the way it did for Kubernetes. “It’s pretty easy these days to say I’m going to bet my company on Kube,” he says. “Nobody’s going to get fired for that.” He hopes OpenShell will get there too.

An unsettled agent stack

The stack for training models is clear, and the one for inference is pretty settled, Bryce says, but for agents it’s “not at all.”

“If there’s not a clear stack, then the industry can’t come together on the most significant problems and actually make really fast, rapid progress,” he says.

Over the next six to 12 months, he expects experimentation to settle into answers on how OpenShell integrates with Kata Containers, gVisor, Agent Substrate, and existing OpenTelemetry projects. Once that happens, he expects agents to take off the way inference has over the last eight months.

Two of those projects are new to the CNCF. Google contributed Agent Substrate, its framework for running long-lived agents on Kubernetes, and the gVisor sandbox runtime at this week’s KubeCon. Nvidia says it’s working with Google on an integration between OpenShell and Agent Substrate.

articles.title: Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator
articles.description: AWS Emulator is a free, open-source local emulator in Rust that lets developers test applications against nearly every AWS service on their own machine using the same CLI and SDK commands, with fidelity measured against real AWS behavior.
articles.content:
Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker.

How it works
You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.

From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region.

The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS.

If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally.

Let’s try it out
To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023. The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so it’s on the path.

PKG=https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest
sudo dnf install -y $PKG/aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm

aws-emulator -v
On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image.

I started the emulator with aws-emulator. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file.

aws-emulator
In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials.

export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://127.0.0.1:9297
export AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/emulator_credentials
export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/config
export AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true
export AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1
unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE
The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR, so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000.

curl --cacert ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health

aws sts get-caller-identity
Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it.

$ aws s3 mb s3://local-getting-started
make_bucket: local-getting-started

$ echo "hello from the emulator" > hello.txt

$ aws s3 cp hello.txt s3://local-getting-started/
upload:./hello.txt to s3://local-getting-started/hello.txt

$ aws s3 ls s3://local-getting-started/
With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them.

Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account.

kiro> Using the local AWS Emulator (the environment variables
are already set in this shell), create a DynamoDB table
"kiro-demo" with a string key "id", put an item
{id: "item-1", msg: "hello from kiro"}, then read it
back with get-item.

$ aws dynamodb create-table --table-name kiro-demo \
--attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S \
--key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH \
--billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

$ aws dynamodb put-item --table-name kiro-demo \
--item '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}, "msg": {"S": "hello from kiro"}}'

$ aws dynamodb get-item --table-name kiro-demo --key '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}}'
To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual.

Using the emulator in process
Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java. For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust. You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process.

use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions};
use aws_sdk_dynamodb::types::{
AttributeDefinition, AttributeValue, BillingMode, KeySchemaElement, KeyType,
ScalarAttributeType,
};

#[tokio::test]
async fn put_then_get_returns_the_item() {
let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default());
let config = aws_config::defaults(aws_config::BehaviorVersion::latest()).http_client(emulator.http_client()).region(aws_config::Region::new("us-east-1")).credentials_provider(emulator.aws_credentials_provider()).load().await;
let ddb = aws_sdk_dynamodb::Client::new(&config);

ddb.create_table().table_name("emulator-demo-table").attribute_definitions(
AttributeDefinition::builder().attribute_name("id").attribute_type(ScalarAttributeType::S).build().unwrap()).key_schema(
KeySchemaElement::builder().attribute_name("id").key_type(KeyType::Hash).build().unwrap()).billing_mode(BillingMode::PayPerRequest).send().await.unwrap();

ddb.put_item().table_name("emulator-demo-table").item("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into())).item("msg", AttributeValue::S("hi".into())).send().await.unwrap();

let got = ddb.get_item().table_name("emulator-demo-table").key("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into())).send().await.unwrap();
assert_eq!(got.item().unwrap().get("msg").unwrap().as_s().unwrap(), "hi");
}
When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off.

How we measure fidelity
An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates.

With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better.

If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

How the emulator is built
AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit, so it stays current with AWS as those models change.

One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository.

How we keep it secure
Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships.

Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

Now available
AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation.

If you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

To get started, see the AWS Emulator documentation.
